easy.heading: Warming Up With A Morning Brew
easy.body:
Starting today's easy puzzle was like catching up with an old friend. I immediately looked for the smallest regions to get some easy wins. The sum target of 2 at cell [0,3] was the perfect place to begin. Since [1,3] was marked as an empty region, I knew the [5,2] domino had to go there, with the 2 landing right on that target. It is always so satisfying when the first piece just clicks into place like that.

Next, I turned my attention to the equals constraint at [2,2] and [2,3]. I had the [6,6] domino sitting there, and it fit like a glove. After that, I had to figure out the big block at the top left that needed to sum to 18. By placing the [0,0] domino at [0,1] and [0,2], and using the 6 from the [3,6] domino and the 0 from the [5,0] domino, everything balanced out perfectly. It just goes to show that even a zero can be a hero when you are trying to hit a specific sum.

medium.heading: Finding My Rhythm In The Middle
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt like a fun dance of doubles. There were so many equal constraints! I noticed right away that I had several double dominoes like [4,4], [2,2], and [5,5]. These are usually the stars of the show in puzzles with lots of equal signs. I spent a few minutes looking at how cells [4,0], [4,1], [4,2], and [4,3] were all connected by these equal requirements. It was like a little chain reaction where one placement determined the next three.

The trickiest part for me was the right side of the board. I had to balance the sum of 6 at cells [2,5] and [3,5] while also making sure the equal constraint at [0,5] and [1,5] worked out. I ended up using the [1,3] and [5,5] dominoes to navigate that corner. Once I realized that cell [0,2] had to be greater than 4, it narrowed my choices down to 5 or 6, which helped me lock in the [0,2] and [0,3] domino to finish the whole grid.

hard.heading: A Real Brain Burner To Finish The Day
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really outdid himself with this hard grid! I felt a bit stumped at first, but then I spotted the zero sum targets at [2,7] and [4,4]. In a game of pips, a zero is a gift because you know exactly what goes there. I paired those up with the [0,0] and [0,1] dominoes to get some traction. The real challenge was that massive unequal region stretching from [3,1] to [5,3]. Seven cells where no two numbers can be the same? That is basically a puzzle all on its own!

I had to be very patient with the bottom of the grid. The sum target of 15 at [5,6], [5,7], and [6,6] required some high-value pips, so I saved my [6,5] and [4,6] dominoes for that area. The breakthrough came when I realized cell [7,8] had to be a 6 to meet its sum target, which forced the [7,7] and [7,8] domino to be the [2,1] or [5,4] pair. It took a bit of back-and-forth, but seeing that final unequal region fill up with 0 through 6 without any repeats was such a great feeling.

explanation.tips: When you are stuck, always look for the regions with a sum of zero or the smallest possible numbers, as they have fewer combinations. Pay close attention to double dominoes because they are your best friends whenever you see an equals constraint. If a region has an unequal constraint, try to keep track of which numbers from 0 to 6 you have already used so you do not accidentally repeat one.
explanation.learned:
Today I learned that unequal regions are much more restrictive than they look. In the hard puzzle, having seven cells in an unequal region meant that every single pip value from 0 to 6 had to appear exactly once. It is a lot like a Sudoku logic trap hidden inside a domino puzzle!

I also realized that when multiple equal constraints are linked together, they form a chain that can clear out a huge section of the board very quickly. It is all about finding that one anchor point to start the chain reaction.

faqs.question: What does the sum constraint mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: A sum constraint is a labeled region where all the pips in those specific cells must add up to the target number shown.

faqs.question: How do you handle an empty region in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region is a cell that does not contribute to any sum or constraint. You still must place a domino pip there, but the value doesn't matter for a target.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be rotated in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, dominoes can be placed either horizontally or vertically to fit the grid and satisfy the constraints.

faqs.question: What is an unequal constraint in a Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: An unequal constraint means that every cell within that specific colored region must have a different pip value from the others.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for the Hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start with the smallest sum targets like 0 or 1, then look for regions with the most constraints, like the equals signs or large unequal blocks.
